Paper Title: A Nigerian Artificial Intelligence Adoption Framework for Education Using the Barrett Model: A Values-Driven, Data Protection–Embedded, Language-Inclusive Blueprint for Teaching and Learning
AI Characteristics: Specifies technical controls like offline-first capabilities for low-connectivity environments.
Task Fit: Identifies AI-supported formative feedback as a use case with high pedagogy fit.
AI Adoption Decision: Defines decision gates, such as infrastructure baselines, for a phased adoption roadmap.
AI Strategy: Framework requires alignment with national education goals through a specific AI Strategy.
AI Use Case Identification: Proposes selecting low-to-moderate risk cases like automated formative feedback.
Data Readiness: Embeds national data protection laws by requiring mandatory DPIAs for high-risk processing.
Organisational Readiness: Identifies power and connectivity as "Survival" level prerequisites for system adoption.
AI Literacy: Proposes teacher micro-credentials in AI pedagogy and literacy modules in certification.
Implementation Coordination: Coordinates adoption via a National Steering Committee and inter-agency DPO networks.
Capability Development: Utilizes iterative pilots and regulatory sandboxes for organizational policy learning.
Sensemaking: Employs the Barrett Model to link technological change with organizational values.
Responsible AI Governance: Defines Ethics and Data Governance Boards with explicit vendor oversight mechanisms.
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Tracks learning gains, accessibility uptake, and teacher workload reduction outcomes.

Paper Title: A UTAUT-Based Framework for Analyzing Users’ Intention to Adopt Artificial Intelligence in Human Resource Recruitment: A Case Study of Thailand
AI Characteristics: Utilizes machine learning for screening, NLP for job postings, and recruitment chatbots.
Task Fit: AI automates tasks like resume matches and onboarding to enhance recruiter focus.
AI Adoption Decision: Finds that perceived autonomy, value, effort expectancy, and facilitating conditions influence adoption.
AI Strategy: Aligns AI recruitment with the "Thailand 4.0" national development strategy.
AI Use Case Identification: Evaluates platforms like HireVue for behavior analysis and Textio for bias reduction.
Organisational Readiness: Facilitating conditions, including perceived resources and support, significantly affect usage intention.
Responsible AI Governance: Emphasizes incorporating AI regulations within Thailand's Personal Data Protection Act.
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI can reduce recruitment time by 90% and increase employment diversity.

Paper Title: A framework to overcome challenges to the adoption of artificial intelligence in Indian Government Organizations
AI Characteristics: Systems are self-learning adaptive algorithms incentivized by reward functions rather than rules.
AI Adoption Decision: Identifies 15 key challenges categorized via the TOE framework.
AI Strategy: Hierarchical model helps policymakers formulate strategies to mitigate AI challenges.
AI Use Case Identification: Surveys uses in granting driving licenses, education loan subsidies, and judicial decisions.
Data Readiness: Finds government data often siloed, fragmented, and un-standardized.
Organisational Readiness: Notes lack of innovation spirit and risk-aversion in the public sector as barriers.
AI Literacy: Highlights lack of capacity and skill as a driving challenge for adoption.
Adaptation/Resistance: Identifies a "mental barrier to change" among frontline managers.
Responsible AI Governance: Finds no accepted standards to measure bias or ethics for public deployment.
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI fills critical personnel gaps in radiodiagnostics and traffic management.

Paper Title: A mixed-methods analysis of artificial intelligence adoption and perceived impacts in Czech municipal administration
AI Characteristics: Distinguishes between language-centric AI (chatbots) and data-centric AI (infrastructure sensors).
Task Fit: Large cities use infrastructure for advanced analysis; smaller towns use text AI for templates.
AI Adoption Decision: Finds that larger municipalities exhibit statistically significantly higher adoption of data-driven AI.
AI Strategy: Comprehensive strategic integration is still in its infancy and often siloed.
AI Use Case Identification: Identifies uses in public waste sensors, traffic management, and transport optimization.
Data Readiness: Identifies fear of data misuse and lack of security guidelines as adoption barriers.
Organisational Readiness: Cites lack of financial and human resources as primary adoption barriers.
Capability Development: Notes smaller municipalities rely on regional analytical outputs due to lack of capacity.
Adaptation/Resistance: Legislative uncertainty breeds caution and apprehension among smaller municipalities.
Routinisation: Finds IT management is the most common entry point for AI across strata.
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Most significant benefit is improved internal efficiency and reduced employee workload.

Paper Title: AI Insurance: How Liability Insurance Can Drive the Responsible Adoption of Artificial Intelligence in Health Care
AI Characteristics: Focuses on software as a medical device (SaMD) and interpretable algorithms.
AI Adoption Decision: Liability risks and legal uncertainty reduce clinician and developer incentives for adoption.
AI Use Case Identification: Notes drug-dosing and surgical assistance systems as specific applications.
Data Readiness: Notes difficulties in accessing high-quality, unbiased training data.
Capability Development: Insurance may require developers to provide ongoing performance data beyond regulatory review.
Responsible AI Governance: Proposes liability insurance to mitigate unpredictable risks and reduce legal uncertainty.
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Insurance products increase trust and help contain the cost of care.

Paper Title: Adopting artificial intelligence in sustainable business
AI Characteristics: AI processes unstructured data into schemas for business intelligence.
Task Fit: AI helps humans disengage from mundane tasks to concentrate on demanding ones.
AI Adoption Decision: AI deployment is interlinked with optimization and pursuit of sustainability benefits.
AI Strategy: Strategic significance of AI is increasing in large Finnish enterprises.
AI Use Case Identification: Identifies uses in hazardous facility inspection robots and forest digital twins.
AI Literacy: AI systems are used to detect and provide for employee training needs.
Capability Development: AI adoption supports personnel engagement and re-allocation to more productive assignments.
Routinisation: AI adoption increased by 12 percent among Finnish firms between 2017-2021.
Responsible AI Governance: Highlights the need for ethical AI auditing and standards for data accuracy.
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI reduces transmission losses in grids, mitigates CO2, and improves ESG footprints.

Paper Title: Adoption of Artificial Intelligence in Organizational Coaching Processes
AI Characteristics: Uses LLMs to personalize dialogue and structure coaching reflections.
Task Fit: Adapts coaching style (S1–S4) based on the coachee's development level.
AI Adoption Decision: Prototyping across multiple LLM services demonstrated operational feasibility.
AI Strategy: Aligns coaching with business strategy by anchoring sessions in organizational context.
AI Use Case Identification: Prototyped scenarios for UX management and developer technical upskilling.
Data Readiness: Adopts "data minimization," requesting only role and goal information.
Organisational Readiness: Organizational approvers validate development proposals to ensure mission alignment.
AI Literacy: AI generates customized KSA triplets to clarify employee learning targets.
Implementation Coordination: Demonstrates automated session orchestration and stateful memory using workflow tools.
Capability Development: OSCAR framework structures dialogue to support human potential and skill building.
Sensemaking: Practitioners judged AI to be helpful in raising coachee situational awareness.
Adaptation/Resistance: Evaluators suggested testing cases with unmotivated or resistant employees.
Routinisation: Embeds a Review step for automated recap and progress check-ins.
Responsible AI Governance: Incorporates disclosure rules, human decision authority, and auditable review logs.
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Generates KPI sets to track development progress and ROI data.

Paper Title: Adoption of artificial intelligence in healthcare: A strategic transformation framework
AI Characteristics: ML prediction models, NLP, and computer vision systems augment clinician decisions.
AI Adoption Decision: Proposes a five-frame journey model: aspire, assess, architect, act, and advance.
AI Strategy: Requires a clear aspiration for intelligent healthcare aligned with organizational purpose.
AI Use Case Identification: Identifies short-term (triage) to long-term (learning health systems) horizons.
Data Readiness: Assess frame evaluates if data architectures are interoperable and high-quality.
Organisational Readiness: Diagnoses readiness across technical, managerial, and behavioral systems via the Iceberg Model.
AI Literacy: Proposes building data science literacy via field and forum learning.
Implementation Coordination: Recommends an AI transformation office to coordinate clinical and technical workstreams.
Capability Development: Gap analysis helps determine whether to build, buy, or partner for skills.
Sensemaking: Narrative linking AI to the mission helps foster workforce conviction.
Adaptation/Resistance: Notes resistance can stem from cognitive overload and "alert fatigue".
Routinisation: Advances change by institutionalising learning systems and after-action reviews.
Responsible AI Governance: Recommends governance defining accountability, override rights, and model drift surveillance.
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Measures impact across initiatives, clinical safety, and enterprise value.

Paper Title: An Analysis of the Readiness of Agricultural Extension Centers in Iraq to Adopt Artificial Intelligence Applications in Integrated Pest and Disease Management
AI Characteristics: AI systems include image-based diagnosis and climate-based algorithm models.
Task Fit: IPM decision support systems minimize pesticide use and optimize spraying.
AI Adoption Decision: Baghdad centers show high readiness due to proximity to institutional support.
AI Strategy: Proposed development strategy aligns institutional capabilities with national digital transformation plans.
AI Use Case Identification: Includes early warning plant health monitoring and border pest detection.
Data Readiness: Notes insufficient data processing capabilities as a barrier to harnessing AI.
Organisational Readiness: Average readiness is "medium," with strengths in willingness but weaknesses in infrastructure.
AI Literacy: Highlights the need for training programs and staff AI skill updates.
Implementation Coordination: Proposes forming technical supervisory committees to monitor administrative challenges.
Capability Development: Prioritizes human resource development as the engine for smart transformation.
Sensemaking: Organizational culture towards innovation is high, reflecting positive attitudes.
Adaptation/Resistance: Identifies resistance to change among some personnel as a moderate threat.
Routinisation: Strategy includes periodic monitoring and evaluation plans across governorates.
Responsible AI Governance: SWOT analysis identifies lack of clarity in national agricultural policies as a threat.
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI supports farmers in making better decisions and achieving sustainable growth.

Paper Title: Adoption of artificial intelligence applications in clinical practice: Insights from a Survey of Healthcare Organizations in Lombardy, Italy
AI Characteristics: Applications focus on analyzing medical images or structured health data.
Task Fit: AI supports diagnostic image analysis and prognostic progression prediction.
AI Adoption Decision: Observed 43% adoption rate; strategies range from commercial purchase to hybrid development.
AI Strategy: Research-focused IRCCS institutes are more likely to engage in AI development.
AI Use Case Identification: Identifies applications prevalent in radiology, oncology, and diabetology.
Data Readiness: Interoperability is a significantly higher barrier for organizations developing AI.
Organisational Readiness: Formal units or structures for AI are rare and limited to development adopters.
AI Literacy: Lack of skilled personnel is the highest-ranked barrier for nonadopters.
Implementation Coordination: Informal initiatives involve multidisciplinary groups or Information Systems departments.
Capability Development: Implementation requires competencies to conduct "make-or-buy" scouting of solutions.
Adaptation/Resistance: Corporate culture is a significant barrier for commercial AI purchasers.
Routinisation: Routinely used applications were CE-marked and integrated into medical devices.
Responsible AI Governance: Privacy concerns were the highest barrier for organizations developing their own applications.
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI applications support diagnosis and prognosis to streamline clinical workflows.

Paper Title: Analyzing Barriers in Adoption of Artificial Intelligence for Resilient Health Care Services to Society
AI Characteristics: Uses machine learning and speech recognition to emulate human capabilities like sense, comprehend, and act (p. 180).
AI Adoption Decision: Prioritizes 18 barriers using DEMATEL; "Inadequate Regulations" is the primary causal driver influencing other adoption factors (p. 186, 192).
AI Strategy: Categorizes barriers into cause-and-effect groups to guide resilient healthcare strategies (p. 181, 189).
AI Use Case Identification: Surveys applications in diabetic retinopathy detection, COVID-19 chatbots, and drug repurposing (p. 180, 181).
Data Readiness: Findings highlight "lack of availability of high-quality data in standardized formats" and "lack of integration" as significant causal barriers (p. 184, 191).
Organisational Readiness: Identifies "High adaptation cost" and "Complexity in managing diversified stakeholders" as significant effects impacted by foundational barriers (p. 189, 191).
AI Literacy: Found "Lack of awareness about AI" as a dominant cause and "shortage of AI expertise" as a critical barrier (p. 189, 192).
Capability Development: Emphasizes the urgent need to "foster AI expertise" and provide "skilling opportunities" to overcome adoption hurdles (p. 192, 193).
Adaptation/Resistance: Notes "Fear among medical specialists of getting replaced by machine" as a cause group barrier (p. 189, 191).
Responsible AI Governance: Identifies inadequate regulations, data privacy, and lack of accountability as high-impact cause-group factors (p. 184, 189).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI adoption aims to boost efficiency and resiliency in India’s healthcare system and improve service quality for society (p. 179, 193).

Paper Title: Antecedents and Outcomes of Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Application in the Workplace: the Socio-Technical System Theory Perspective
AI Characteristics: Machines performing cognitive functions like learning and problem-solving, able to sense, reason, and respond (p. 2).
Task Fit: Model proposes that desired individual and organisational outcomes depend on the fit between social and technical subsystems (p. 11).
AI Adoption Decision: Proposes that adoption is jointly influenced by personnel, technical, organisational structure, and external environment subsystems (p. 12, 14, 16, 17).
AI Strategy: Transformative success requires aligning AI strategy and operating models with organizational objectives (p. 11).
Data Readiness: Identifies technological resources like "data" as critical for readiness and adoption (p. 13).
Organisational Readiness: "Technology readiness" and organisational structure factors (leadership support, culture) are proposed as critical antecedents (p. 11, 13).
AI Literacy: Training and technical knowledge are identified as key factors for implementation and scaling AI responsibly (p. 14).
Implementation Coordination: Recommends that managers build effective management mechanisms and project teams to support adoption (p. 25).
Capability Development: Organizations should develop "adaptive competencies" and reskill employees to work alongside AI (p. 25, 27).
Adaptation/Resistance: Notes turnover intention and perceived job risk as negative individual outcomes of replacement intention (p. 17, 18).
Routinisation: Emphasizes institutionalizing AI by embedding best practices at the organizational level to change operations (p. 14).
Responsible AI Governance: Suggests developing a code of ethics and monitoring security, bias, and privacy via government regulations (p. 16).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Proposed outcomes include improved labor effectiveness, operational efficiency, and customer service quality (p. 19, 20).

Paper Title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Adoption and Enterprise Risk Management (ERM): The Roles of Information Technology (IT) Infrastructure Flexibility, Technology Competence, and Organizational Culture in Ghana
AI Characteristics: Automated data analysis, substantive testing, and continuous monitoring via machine learning and predictive analytics (p. 2).
Task Fit: AI tools automate routine auditing tasks and detect anomalous patterns traditional sampling might miss (p. 2, 21).
AI Adoption Decision: SEM results confirm AI adoption significantly influences ERM and IT infrastructure flexibility (p. 16).
AI Strategy: Emphasizes the need for strategic alignment between AI investments and organizational capabilities to realize value (p. 1).
AI Use Case Identification: Identifies anomaly detection, fraud assessment, and real-time modeling of risk scenarios as key applications (p. 5).
Data Readiness: Compliance with regulations like the Data Protection Act safeguards data integrity and enables real-time reporting (p. 21).
Organisational Readiness: Findings suggest that organizational culture, emphasizing accountability and innovation, enhances the effective use of flexible IT tools (p. 20).
AI Literacy: Managerial expertise and specialized training in AI are identified as necessary to oversee AI-driven auditing (p. 11, 21).
Implementation Coordination: Recommends establishing interdisciplinary teams to consistently monitor and optimize AI systems (p. 21).
Capability Development: Building "technology competencies" significantly strengthens the relationship between AI adoption and ERM performance (p. 1, 16).
Routinisation: AI integration encourages adaptable IT systems, facilitating a shift from periodic to continuous real-time risk monitoring (p. 5, 16).
Responsible AI Governance: Highlights compliance with Ghanaian corporate governance and Data Protection Act to ensure ethical automation (p. 18, 21).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI adoption boosts operational resilience, audit quality, and productivity while strengthening client trust (p. 2, 3).

Paper Title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption by SMEs to Achieve Sustainable Business Performance: Application of Technology–Organization– Environment Framework
AI Characteristics: Machine learning, deep learning, NLP, and image recognition used to transform data into actionable decisions (p. 1).
Task Fit: AI automates repetitive tasks to increase productivity and meet work requirements (p. 6, 7).
AI Adoption Decision: Factors like relative advantage, compatibility, sustainable human capital, and government support significantly influence adoption (p. 1, 14).
AI Strategy: AI adoption is linked to Vision 2030 modernization initiatives to achieve sustainable innovation and competitiveness (p. 9, 16).
AI Use Case Identification: Identifies uses in green manufacturing, packaging design, and customer behavior prediction (p. 6, 15).
Data Readiness: AI empowers people to systematize disaggregated information and transform large datasets into decisions (p. 1).
Organisational Readiness: "Sustainable human capital" has a significant impact on adoption, while general "organizational support" was insignificant in Saudi SMEs (p. 14).
AI Literacy: Workforce skills and employee readiness are potential plus points for accepting AI and other innovations (p. 16).
Capability Development: Emphasizes investing in capacity-building and training employees to manage advanced technologies (p. 15, 16).
Adaptation/Resistance: Notes that complexity can be a fundamental problem leading to reluctance or sensitivity to errors (p. 4, 15).
Responsible AI Governance: Recommends including ethical concerns as part of sustainable HR practices for responsible AI administration (p. 18).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI adoption positively and significantly impacts operational efficiency, product quality, and economic performance (p. 14).

Paper Title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption for Sustainable Growth in SMEs: An Extended Dynamic Capability Framework
AI Characteristics: AI solutions include predictive analytics, process automation, and chatbots for customer engagement (p. 5, 27).
Task Fit: AI complements innovation efforts by automating routine tasks and enabling faster responsiveness to market demands (p. 22).
AI Adoption Decision: Dynamic capabilities (sensing, seizing, transforming) positively influence AI Adoption Intensity and AI Acceptance Rate (p. 11, 20).
AI Strategy: AI adoption represents a strategic lever for innovation-driven growth and long-term firm sustainability (p. 22).
AI Use Case Identification: Lists use cases in market research, product portfolio management, and cybersecurity defenses (p. 5).
Data Readiness: Ready adoption of cloud platforms enhances storage and processing efficiency for seamless AI integration (p. 8).
Organisational Readiness: Organizational readiness and openness to change are highlighted as enablers for scaling AI solutions (p. 5).
AI Literacy: Suggests targeted AI training programs to improve general digital literacy across functional roles (p. 24, 25).
Implementation Coordination: Creation of cross-functional AI task forces is recommended to align implementation with business needs (p. 24).
Capability Development: Well-developed dynamic capabilities enable firms to adapt and reorganize resources for AI adoption (p. 1, 13).
Adaptation/Resistance: Cultivating AI champions and integrating AI into the company vision helps reduce resistance (p. 25).
Routinisation: Emphasizes "AI Adoption Intensity," representing the extent AI is integrated and substantially changes business processes (p. 27, 23).
Responsible AI Governance: Emphasizes training focused on ethical AI use to foster long-term transformation (p. 25).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI adoption intensity positively influences technological, economic, and collaborative performance (p. 11, 20).

Paper Title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption, Innovation Efficiency, and Governance Mechanisms: Evidence from China
AI Characteristics: Key technologies include NLP, computer vision, neural networks, and generative AI (p. 5, 7).
Task Fit: AI reconstructs R&D models by optimizing search, representation, and aggregation in repetitive, information-intensive tasks (p. 5).
AI Adoption Decision: Regression analysis shows AI adoption significantly improves enterprise innovation efficiency (p. 12).
AI Strategy: Enterprises should define the strategic positioning of AI within innovation systems to achieve data-driven mechanisms (p. 20).
AI Use Case Identification: Identifies R&D decision-making, product design, and market decision-making as key application areas (p. 1, 5).
Data Readiness: AI provides a foundation for innovation through data mining and knowledge integration mechanisms (p. 5).
Organisational Readiness: Digital Leadership and executives with digital acumen act as catalysts for effective integration (p. 4).
AI Literacy: "Executives’ digital background" serves as a bridge, reducing technical and cognitive barriers for AI adoption (p. 5, 19).
Implementation Coordination: EDB promotes cross-departmental collaboration and knowledge sharing, reducing technology silos (p. 5).
Capability Development: AI adoption enhances firms' dynamic capabilities to sense, seize, and reconfigure market opportunities (p. 5).
Adaptation/Resistance: Digital leaders foster an open innovation atmosphere that enhances employee acceptance of AI (p. 5).
Routinisation: Embedding AI into innovation paradigms reshapes models for research, development, and process management (p. 1, 20).
Responsible AI Governance: External governance via media attention improves transparency and provides reputational pressure for responsible adoption (p. 13, 19).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI adoption significantly boosts innovation efficiency (ln(patent)/ln(R&D investment)) and resource allocation efficiency (p. 1, 19).

Paper Title: Artificial intelligence adoption as a mediator of executive cultural diversity-ESG performance nexus: evidence from European companies
AI Characteristics: Uses natural language processing (NLP) to replicate human cognitive functions like perception and decision-making (p. 4).
Task Fit: AI facilitates consensus by systematically integrating varied cultural perspectives into actionable ESG strategies (p. 2).
AI Adoption Decision: SEM analysis shows that "executive cultural diversity" positively influences AI adoption at the 1% level (p. 10, 12).
AI Strategy: AI adoption should be strategically aligned with cultural diversity to refine ESG strategies and outcomes (p. 1, 13).
AI Use Case Identification: Identifies uses in energy management, workforce diversity monitoring, and fraud detection (p. 3, 11).
Data Readiness: AI processes vast unstructured data and improves reporting accuracy through real-time monitoring (p. 1, 11).
Organisational Readiness: Culturally diverse leadership teams are found to be a valuable strategic resource for Europe's AI transformation (p. 10, 13).
AI Literacy: Leaders promote "AI awareness" and implement tailored training to identify and address skill gaps (p. 4).
Implementation Coordination: AI helps leaders analyze, coordinate, and refine complex responses across multicultural business environments (p. 5, 13).
Capability Development: Culturally diverse teams foster innovation and attract international talent, creating unique synergetic advantages (p. 10, 13).
Routinisation: AI is positioned as a tool to automate compliance and integrate sustainability into corporate strategy (p. 3, 11).
Responsible AI Governance: Emphasizes using AI to ensure compliance with the EU AI Act and Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI (p. 2, 10).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI adoption improves ESG performance scores and enhances stakeholder trust (p. 1, 11).

Paper Title: Artificial intelligence adoption in the service industry
AI Characteristics: AI automates routine processes like daily document handling and simplified management (p. 2).
AI Adoption Decision: Positive associations found between perceived usefulness, ease of use, and intention to adopt AI (p. 1, 13).
AI Strategy: Suggests development of ethical AI adoption strategies to ensure proper integration among frontline employees (p. 1).
AI Use Case Identification: AI is used for community engagement through digital platforms and document handling (p. 2).
Data Readiness: Concerns about privacy in data collection, submitting information to AI, or unauthorized access were assessed (p. 4, 6).
Organisational Readiness: Assessment of "Leadership support" as a moderator showed no significant impact on the adoption path (p. 10, 13).
AI Literacy: Prior experience with AI is an important predictor of adoption; age has a negative effect (p. 1, 14).
Sensemaking: Intuitive communication and trust shape employee perceptions of usefulness and ease of use (p. 1, 14).
Adaptation/Resistance: Evaluates performance anxiety and communication barriers that hinder user interaction with AI systems (p. 4, 6).
Routinisation: AI already in the workplace for 56% of respondents, automating and simplifying service provision (p. 12).
Responsible AI Governance: Evaluates employees' concerns about performance risks, privacy, and bias in AI integration (p. 1, 4).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI adoption aims to make service provision more efficient, accurate, and cost-effective (p. 1, 2).

Paper Title: Artificial intelligence and blockchain adoption for sustainable financial performance: The mediating role of DAC in Jordanian financial institutions
AI Characteristics: Focuses on Machine Learning Capability (intelligent algorithms) and Intelligent Decision-Making Systems (p. 668, 669).
AI Adoption Decision: PLS-SEM reveals AI and blockchain adoption positively and significantly influence sustainable financial performance (p. 666, 672).
AI Strategy: AI and blockchain are introduced into strategies to fortify competitive advantage and operational resilience (p. 667, 674).
AI Use Case Identification: Uses in fraud detection, customer profiling, and predictive financial modeling (p. 668, 669).
Data Readiness: Data Analytics Capability (DAC) refers to the ability to gather and process large volumes of financial data (p. 669, 670).
Organisational Readiness: Analytical frameworks and support mechanisms are required to ensure technology implementation leads to benefits (p. 671, 674).
AI Literacy: DAC enables institutions to convert digital information into strategic knowledge and evidence-based management (p. 669, 670).
Implementation Coordination: AI and blockchain adoption requires integration processes and automated data coordination (p. 667, 674).
Capability Development: Strong analytical skills boost institutional agility, operational responsiveness, and financial innovation performance (p. 668, 672).
Adaptation/Resistance: Notes "organisational resistance" may impact short-term financial sustainability during machine learning adoption (p. 671, 674).
Routinisation: AI technologies become strategic assets when effectively embedded within organizational systems and activities (p. 670, 671).
Responsible AI Governance: Emphasizes blockchain platforms for transaction security, transparency, and digital financial reliability (p. 667, 671).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI adoption improves operational efficiency, transaction transparency, and long-term financial resilience (p. 666, 672).

Paper Title: Artificial intelligence in agriculture across south Asia: Technology adoption, improvements, and sustainability outcomes
AI Characteristics: Key technologies include machine learning, image recognition, spectral analysis, and predictive algorithms (p. 11, 14).
Task Fit: AI-enabled precision agriculture (smart irrigation, sensor monitoring) helps farmers pursue growth and efficiency (p. 8, 10).
AI Adoption Decision: Adoption varies: India/Sri Lanka are institution-led (DOI), while Bangladesh/Nepal depend on individual behavioral acceptance (TAM) (p. 2, 10).
AI Strategy: Policymakers should design strategies to enhance digital infrastructure and promote inclusive financing (p. 12).
AI Use Case Identification: Identifies 6 functional categories: Crop Planning, Pest Management, Soil Optimization, Supply Chain, Financial Inclusion, Quality Control (p. 7).
Data Readiness: AI-driven analytics improve predictive precision even under uncertainty and incomplete data (p. 8).
Organisational Readiness: Findings reveal that infrastructure readiness and institutional coordination are decisive factors for scaling AI (p. 2).
AI Literacy: Adoption in Bangladesh and Nepal is significantly influenced by digital literacy and farmers' technological confidence (p. 2, 10).
Implementation Coordination: Cross-border public-private collaborations are recommended to accelerate data-driven transformation (p. 2).
Capability Development: Emphasizes region-wide investment in rural digital infrastructure and AI literacy to build human capital (p. 2, 12).
Sensemaking: TAM-based countries rely on farmers' "perceptions of usefulness" and ease of use to determine engagement (p. 2, 10).
Routinisation: AI is integrated through mobile-based advisory systems and automated procurement/payment platforms (p. 11, 13).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI implementation reduces water use (15%) and fertilizer use (10%) while maintaining production (p. 11, 15).

Paper Title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption in Sustainability Reporting: Opportunities and Challenges for African Small-Medium Entreprises
AI Characteristics: Key technologies include natural language processing (NLP), machine learning (ML), and predictive analytics (p. 2, 14).
Task Fit: AI's strategic value emerges from integration with firm-specific resources like digital infrastructure (p. 2, 13).
AI Adoption Decision: Adoption decision depends on "resource readiness" between established digital systems versus those lacking them (p. 2).
AI Strategy: SMEs can develop targeted digital strategies to ensure compliance and position themselves competitively (p. 3, 15).
AI Use Case Identification: Identifies uses in ESG data collection automation, carbon footprint calculation, and risk modeling (p. 4, 9, 20).
Data Readiness: Fragmentation, informality, and non-digitized operational data are identified as critical challenges for adoption (p. 1, 13).
Organisational Readiness: Infrastructural equity and weak institutional support are identified as external barriers to readiness (p. 1, 15).
AI Literacy: Identifies low levels of digital literacy and human capital shortages as primary obstacles to implementation (p. 4, 11).
Implementation Coordination: Emphasizes cross-functional coordination to avoid superficial compliance and ensure internal comprehension (p. 13, 14).
Capability Development: SMEs must invest in "capability formation" and tailored training programs to activate AI resources effectively (p. 12, 14).
Sensemaking: Librarians in qualitative interviews report "trusting the software blindly" due to technical complexity (p. 12).
Adaptation/Resistance: Fragmented data and informality make AI tools ineffective, leading to exclusion from ESH demands (p. 13).
Routinisation: AI adoption is described as contingent on being "embedded in firm-specific routines" to create sustained advantage (p. 2, 5).
Responsible AI Governance: Emphasizes governance mechanisms, data privacy, and ethical standards for data validation and oversight (p. 2, 14).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Opportunities include resource optimization, competitive differentiation, and improved Organizational performance and accuracy (p. 1, 9, 10).

Paper Title: Artificial Intelligence in German Robo-Advisory: A Qualitative Examination of Adoption and Future Prospects
AI Characteristics: Advanced techniques include machine learning, neural networks, and sophisticated ESG screening (p. 747, 749).
Task Fit: RAs use AI to supplement human expertise, enabling optimized investment strategies (p. 754).
AI Adoption Decision: Actual adoption rates (11.1%) lag behind hype due to regulatory hurdles, data privacy, and high R&D costs (p. 746, 757).
AI Strategy: Pioneering firms use AI as a "key differentiator" to carve out niche brand identities in a fragmented market (p. 756, 757).
AI Use Case Identification: Includes automated portfolio rebalancing, predictive market analytics, and AI-powered client onboarding chatbots (p. 749, 759).
Data Readiness: Emphasizes firm strength in "handling large datasets" to offer robust risk management (p. 757).
Organisational Readiness: Shortage of skilled professionals and limited in-house technical expertise are identified as internal weaknesses (p. 746, 760, 761).
AI Literacy: Practical recommendations include investing in "employee training" to mitigate the talent gap (p. 746).
Implementation Coordination: Proposes collaboration with partners to streamline implementation processes and accelerate learning (p. 747, 763).
Capability Development: Pioneering firms develop complex machine learning capabilities to gain a competitive edge (p. 761, 762).
Sensemaking: Interviews reveal CEO skepticism around "fully automated decisions" due to market unpredictability (p. 759, 761).
Adaptation/Resistance: German public’s aversion to risk and "AI skepticism" might limit uptake of advanced strategies (p. 759, 760).
Routinisation: AI-supported models supplement human investment committees to build ongoing managed portfolios (p. 747, 754).
Responsible AI Governance: Recommends adopting robust governance frameworks to ensure data handling is secure and decisions are explainable (p. 747, 762).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI aims to democratise finance, improve investor outcomes, and provide higher-quality customer engagement (p. 747, 759).

Paper Title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption for Sustainable Audit Quality in Non-Big Four Accounting Firm
AI Characteristics: Key functional features include anomaly detection algorithms and predictive analytics (p. 20).
Task Fit: AI improves quality by freeing auditors' time from tedious data input for judgment-based work (p. 20, 22).
AI Adoption Decision: UTAUT model shows performance expectancy (β=0.537) and effort expectancy (β=0.612) are significant factors (p. 20, 24).
AI Strategy: AI adoption is seen as a driver to maintain audit quality and competitiveness in a technologically advanced setting (p. 20).
AI Use Case Identification: Evaluated for fraud risk identification, checking accuracy of electronic files, and re-do procedures (p. 21, 22).
Data Readiness: AI enables auditors to effectively examine "big datasets" to spot irregularities traditional methods miss (p. 20, 22).
Organisational Readiness: Conservative organizational cultures and lack of resources in smaller firms are noted as barriers (p. 20).
AI Literacy: Lack of experience is a challenge, emphasizing the need for targeted training to promote adoption (p. 20).
Implementation Coordination: Organizational support is needed to drive AI integration and reduce psychological barriers (p. 20, 21).
Capability Development: Professional skepticism is aided by AI, increasing auditors' understanding of client entities (p. 22, 24).
Sensemaking: Auditors' performance and effort expectations are the primary cognitive drivers influencing usage intention (p. 20, 24).
Adaptation/Resistance: Notes smaller businesses face "doubts about the ROI" of AI investments, hindering uptake (p. 20).
Routinisation: AI automates reconciliation and journal entry testing, embedding technology into standard audit workflows (p. 20, 21).
Responsible AI Governance: Adoption ensures audits satisfy legal requirements and maintain the integrity of financial statements (p. 20).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI adoption dramatically improves sustainable audit quality and auditor productivity (p. 24).

Paper Title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption, Green HRM, and Employee Behavior: Driving Environmental Sustainability in SMEs with Organizational Culture as a Moderator
AI Characteristics: Key features include machine learning, NLP, data analytics, and real-time monitoring (p. 2, 4).
Task Fit: AI assists SMEs in adapting operations to sustainability-focused models and reducing environmental strain (p. 5, 12).
AI Adoption Decision: PLS-SEM confirms AI adoption significantly enhances environmental sustainability directly (p. 1, 10).
AI Strategy: AI enables organizations to align business processes with global sustainability standards and green HRM goals (p. 2, 12).
AI Use Case Identification: Includes energy efficiency monitoring, waste reduction tracking, and AI-powered gamified training platforms (p. 2, 3).
Data Readiness: Real-time monitoring and data analytics help optimize energy consumption and lower carbon footprints (p. 4, 12).
Organisational Readiness: Barriers like lack of digital infrastructure and resistance to change impact readiness in Pakistani SMEs (p. 6).
AI Literacy: AI's ability to "personalize training" helps educate employees on sustainability initiatives and behaviors (p. 8, 12).
Implementation Coordination: AI adoption acts as a technological equalizer to reconfigure operations without large-scale overhaul (p. 12, 13).
Capability Development: Sustainable growth results from alignment of technological capabilities with human engagement and cultural support (p. 14).
Sensemaking: High pro-environmental culture ensures that AI-driven strategies are successfully implemented and durable (p. 9, 13).
Adaptation/Resistance: Resistance to change and implementation costs are identified as double-edged challenges in smaller firms (p. 6, 14).
Routinisation: AI-driven GHRM practices embed environmental awareness into firm routines like performance evaluation (p. 13, 15).
Responsible AI Governance: Future research suggested for "ethical dimensions" like algorithmic bias, data privacy, and transparency (p. 14).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI-driven systems reduced energy consumption by 25% within one year in Pakistan's manufacturing sector (p. 5, 10).

Paper Title: Artificial intelligence competency and ethical considerations: Strategies for sustainable adoption among librarians in the fifth industrial revolution
AI Characteristics: Generative AI tools like ChatGPT and Grammarly are used for content generation and plagiarism detection (p. 1, 8, 14).
Task Fit: Successful adoption depends on the alignment between AI tools and librarians’ everyday professional tasks (p. 5, 12).
AI Adoption Decision: Adoption is limited by infrastructural deficits, inconsistent access, and outdated professional training (p. 2, 16).
AI Strategy: Proposes a holistic strategy encompassing institutional policy, inclusive training, and localisation of tools (p. 1, 12).
AI Use Case Identification: Identifies categories: content generation, plagiarism detection, literature analysis, and language enhancement (p. 6).
Data Readiness: Ethical concerns center on risk of data breaches and weak data governance in cloud-based tools (p. 10).
Organisational Readiness: Poor digital infrastructure and limited institutional funding are significant structural barriers (p. 11, 12).
AI Literacy: Librarians report proficiency in language tools but noticeable gaps in competence for literature analysis (p. 10, 13).
Implementation Coordination: Calls for AI Ethics Committees and Governance Boards to foster informed, proactive leadership (p. 12, 13).
Capability Development: Proposes intensive training to build digital competence and AI literacy across all professional ranks (p. 12, 13).
Sensemaking: Librarians prioritize tools based on perceived usefulness for academic writing and user services (p. 12, 13).
Adaptation/Resistance: Librarians expressed hesitation and fear of misuse due to lack of ethical professional standards (p. 13, 16).
Routinisation: Language tools like Grammarly are used daily by over 50% of respondents, becoming part of workflows (p. 12).
Responsible AI Governance: Emphasizes data protection, academic integrity, and cultural insensitivity as core ethical adoption principles (p. 1, 10).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI tools optimize academic service delivery, research support, and streamline administrative workflows (p. 1, 2).

Paper Title: Assessing the nexus of Generative AI adoption, ethical considerations and organizational performance
AI Characteristics: GenAI incorporates ML models and Natural Language Processing (NLP) to generate new content like text and images (p. 3).
AI Adoption Decision: Use is significantly influenced by coercive, normative, and mimetic institutional pressures from stakeholders (p. 2, 50).
Data Readiness: Accuracy of output is found to be a significant predictor of the use of GenAI (p. 41).
Organisational Readiness: Organizational innovativeness significantly moderates the relationship between GenAI use and performance (p. 2, 41, 53).
Responsible AI Governance: Fairness, accountability, transparency, and autonomy are critical ethical principles influencing adoption (p. 2, 40-41, 51).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Use of GenAI significantly and positively impacts organizational performance (β = 0.348) (p. 41, 53).

Paper Title: Be ethical then proficient: navigating employees’ ethical adoption of generative AI in the workplace
Task Fit: Proficiency is defined as applying GenAI thoughtfully to meet specific work objectives and responsibilities (p. 169).
AI Adoption Decision: Defines ethical adoption as the employee’s ability to be aware of responsibilities and risks during tasks (p. 139).
AI Strategy: Leadership clearly communicating the vision and direction for work goals empowers employees to apply AI (p. 143).
Organisational Readiness: Change leadership (issue-focused guidance) significantly promotes employees' ethical adoption of GenAI (p. 169, 170).
AI Literacy: AI ethics is identified as one of the four core dimensions of AI literacy (p. 139).
Implementation Coordination: Dynamic participation and feedback during training are critical to ensure desirable outcomes (p. 169, 171).
Capability Development: Ethical adoption of GenAI leads to significantly higher proficient use of the technology on the job (p. 169).
Sensemaking: Transparent communication helps reduce misunderstandings, anxiety, and confusion about GenAI changes (p. 141).
Responsible AI Governance: Transparent communication (substantiality, participation, accountability) during training fosters ethical adoption (p. 136, 141).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Older individuals are more likely to ethically adopt AI but feel less confident using it proficiently (p. 151).

Paper Title: Beyond Automation: Ethical and Professional Dimensions of Artificial Intelligence Adoption in UAE Government Communication
AI Characteristics: Identified tools include predictive analytics, chatbots, automated translation, and sentiment monitoring (p. 194).
Task Fit: AI is widely viewed as a transformational tool that enhances communication effectiveness and responsiveness (p. 194).
AI Adoption Decision: Adoption is driven by perceived usefulness, ease of use, ethical value, and cultural orientations (p. 193, 202, 271).
AI Strategy: AI tools and implementation efforts align with national initiatives like the UAE AI Strategy 2031 (p. 195, 242).
AI Use Case Identification: Applications include social media monitoring, citizen engagement, and automated reporting (p. 201, 239).
Data Readiness: Lack of high-quality data and data privacy restrictions are identified as critical barriers (p. 195, 252).
Organisational Readiness: Significant barriers include organizational resistance, skill gaps among graduates, and financial constraints (p. 195, 264, 266).
AI Literacy: Implementation requires investment in training to address digital literacy and expertise gaps (p. 196, 251, 266).
Implementation Coordination: Emphasizes the need for cross-departmental collaboration and strategic partnerships with academic institutions (p. 196, 244).
Capability Development: AI is conceptualized as a complement to human expertise rather than a replacement (p. 195, 242).
Sensemaking: Professionals acknowledge potential but are guarded by reliability problems and fear of job displacement (p. 201, 266).
Adaptation/Resistance: Observed cultural resistance and a "mindset" sticking to traditional ways among some officials (p. 250, 252).
Routinisation: Larger government media offices lead adoption, while smaller emirates are still scaling capabilities (p. 203, 264).
Responsible AI Governance: Ethical governance must prioritize transparency, accountability, and cultural sensitivity to identity/values (p. 195, 254, 268).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI improves communication efficiency and facilitates more data-driven decision-making for citizen services (p. 211, 275).

Paper Title: Challenges To Adopting Artificial Intelligence Technologies For The Development Of Smart Governance Of Smart City
AI Characteristics: Incorporates technologies for digital workplaces, intelligent power systems, and information encryption (p. 304).
Task Fit: AI optimizes infrastructure design, route planning, and demand-side grid flexibility (p. 307).
AI Adoption Decision: DEMATEL model prioritizes "Data Privacy and Security" as the primary causal obstacle to adoption (p. 310).
AI Strategy: Requires strategic planning, innovative leadership, and budget distribution to surmount obstacles (p. 311, 312).
AI Use Case Identification: Identified uses in traffic congestion, water scarcity, pollution, and trash management (p. 306).
Data Readiness: Intricacy of incorporating AI into outdated governance frameworks and training on extensive datasets are hurdles (p. 310, 311).
Organisational Readiness: Limited financial resources and outdated infrastructure are significant structural obstacles (p. 310, 311).
AI Literacy: Insufficient comprehension and proficiency of government officials hinder effective decision-making (p. 310).
Implementation Coordination: Absence of standardized protocols hinders smooth interaction between AI systems and tech platforms (p. 311).
Routinisation: Resistance from government bodies is identified as a key obstacle to implementing smart governance (p. 310).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Implementation raises concerns about bias, discrimination, surveillance, and human rights infringements (p. 306).

Paper Title: Corporate Social Responsibility Practices, Managerial Attitudes Toward Artificial Intelligence, and AI Adoption in Micro and Small Restaurant SMEs
AI Characteristics: Uses the EU definition: machine-based systems operating with varying levels of autonomy (p. 321).
Task Fit: AI is primarily associated with everyday administrative, planning, or customer-facing tasks (p. 368, 369).
AI Adoption Decision: Positive managerial attitudes are the key driver; financial performance acts as a boundary condition (p. 320, 363, 370).
AI Use Case Identification: Tools include online booking/food ordering, interactive chatbots, CRM, and virtual assistants (p. 369, 384).
Organisational Readiness: Financial differences reflect in adoption intensity; lower-revenue firms may have more centralized decision-making (p. 371).
AI Literacy: Structural constraints and skill shortages are identified as significant barriers in restaurant SMEs (p. 323, 332).
Sensemaking: Managers prioritize service authenticity and express concerns about the loss of human interaction (p. 323, 330).
Adaptation/Resistance: Environmental CSR practices are negatively associated with AI attitudes, reflecting cautious evaluations (p. 320, 362, 368).
Routinisation: AI adoption remains uneven and selective, used cautiously for operational rather than strategic integration (p. 366).
Responsible AI Governance: Employee-related CSR practices are institutionalized baseline norms and do not differentiate attitudes toward AI (p. 320, 367).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Financial performance (revenue) is not a direct outcome but a contextual factor shaping adoption decisions (p. 320, 361).

Paper Title: Critical success factors influencing artificial intelligence adoption in food supply chains
AI Characteristics: AI encompasses programs, algorithms, and machines designed to imitate human behavior for problem-solving (p. 405).
Task Fit: AI interventions address unique food sector challenges like product perishability and quality deterioration (p. 409, 412).
AI Adoption Decision: Top critical factors include technology readiness, security, privacy, and customer satisfaction (p. 404, 453).
AI Strategy: A clear linkage between vision and strategy is a key organizational critical success factor (p. 417, 446).
AI Use Case Identification: Used for real-time tracking information to minimize shipment challenges and production yields (p. 413, 452).
Data Readiness: Sufficient security and privacy for data protection are the second-ranked technological sub-dimensions (p. 439, 442).
Organisational Readiness: Adequate top management support and establishing sufficient organizational resources are critical enablers (p. 417, 446).
AI Literacy: Proper training for staff and end-users is an influential human-dimension success factor (p. 419, 445).
Implementation Coordination: Information sharing and communication among supply chain partners are vital for adopting AI (p. 419, 445).
Sensemaking: Institutional trust (beliefs about safety) is identified as a prominent environmental success factor (p. 418, 443).
Adaptation/Resistance: Behavioral change management initiatives are required to facilitate organizational adoption (p. 417, 442).
Routinisation: AI integration in the Indian food supply chain is still in the nascent phase (p. 453).
Responsible AI Governance: Regulatory compliance and ethics in data collection are significant environmental factors for adoption (p. 418, 439).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Customer satisfaction achieved through error reduction and better traceability is a primary human factor (p. 445).

Paper Title: Curse or Blessing: Investigating the Influence of Firms’ Artificial Intelligence Adoption on Employee Job Satisfaction
AI Characteristics: Adoption shifts the focus from augmentation (human-AI collaboration) to automation (autonomous decisions) (p. 506, 507).
Task Fit: Automation handles structured "monkey tasks," while humans handle difficult, unstructured, and creative tasks (p. 506, 586).
AI Adoption Decision: Relationship between adoption and job satisfaction is an inverted U-shape; satisfaction peaks at moderate adoption (p. 494, 583).
AI Strategy: Exploration orientation (innovation focus) shifts the peak satisfaction point to higher levels of adoption (p. 494, 556, 583).
AI Use Case Identification: Evaluation covers demand forecasting, virtual agents, and robotic process automation (p. 596).
Organisational Readiness: Firms with higher exploration orientation realize greater job enrichment and handle higher adoption levels (p. 519, 591).
AI Literacy: Employees must reorient themselves by learning new skills to excel in tasks requiring human elements (p. 590).
Sensemaking: Employees view AI as both a helpful collaborator and a potential adversary (p. 586).
Adaptation/Resistance: Resistance stems from role disorientation, occupational identity threats, and fears of displacement (p. 516, 525).
Routinisation: AI adoption manifests by changing job characteristics—complexity and autonomy—rather than creating new jobs (p. 502, 590).
Responsible AI Governance: Pronounced data governance (quality/availability management) flattens the curve of the AI-job satisfaction relationship (p. 500, 559).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: At high adoption levels, impairment effects (information overload, deskilling) outweigh enrichment benefits, reducing satisfaction (p. 516, 588).

Paper Title: Development and validation of the generative artificial intelligence appropriation (GAIA) Scale: A comprehensive measurement tool for assessing user engagement and utilisation
AI Characteristics: GAI produces human-like content and learns from user interactions and prompts (p. 638, 640).
Task Fit: Appropriation depends on how well social and technological structures are jointly optimized (p. 646).
AI Adoption Decision: Adoption constitutes an elemental step, representing the interest in and intention to use AI (p. 651, 692).
AI Strategy: Scale provides a roadmap for professionals to achieve strategic goals through effective AI use (p. 643, 649).
AI Use Case Identification: Used for everyday work tasks like problem-solving, decision-making, time management, and brainstorming (p. 691).
Organisational Readiness: Empowerment climate and technology platform quality are structural antecedents to appropriation (p. 655).
AI Literacy: Professional training programs should be tailored to the individual's level of appropriation (p. 700).
Capability Development: Appropriation aids in the development of skills, knowledge, and organizational competencies (p. 653).
Sensemaking: Appropriation reflects users’ efforts to create their own sense of the technology (p. 654).
Adaptation/Resistance: Customised appropriation involves user-centric "workarounds" and reconfiguration outside envisioned usage (p. 642, 693, 695, 701).
Routinisation: Integrative appropriation captures how users embed tools into everyday organizational routines and practices (p. 653, 691).
Responsible AI Governance: Ethical appropriation measures the ethical or unethical intent behind using technology beyond developer intent (p. 697, 698).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: High levels of GAIA positively and significantly influence individual creative performance (ICP) (p. 689).

Paper Title: Employee adoption of artificial intelligence systems in the electrical and electronics industry: a hybrid PLS–fsQCA analysis
AI Characteristics: AI system features include reliability, explainability, intelligibility, and adaptability (p. 792).
Task Fit: Task-technology fit significantly predicts adoption intention; technology adaptability determines fit more than task variability (p. 766, 817, 834).
AI Adoption Decision: Intention is driven by performance expectancy, fit, social influence, and personal innovativeness (p. 766, 816, 834).
AI Strategy: E&E context represents a digitally ambidextrous environment where AI enhances professional capability (p. 821, 839).
AI Use Case Identification: Applications include data classification, trend detection, and predictive analytics (p. 791).
Data Readiness: Institutionalized basic infrastructure (IT support, connectivity) acts as a hygiene factor rather than a motivator (p. 824).
Organisational Readiness: Leadership commitment and innovation-friendly cultures encourage experimentation and reduce fear (p. 785).
AI Literacy: Recommends continuous reskilling programs and peer knowledge-sharing to sustain long-term engagement (p. 839).
Implementation Coordination: Transparent communication and participatory implementation strategies mitigate perceived threats (p. 820, 835).
Capability Development: AI is perceived as augmentative to cognitive and analytical capabilities (p. 824).
Sensemaking: Employees acknowledgment of potential is tempered by job replacement anxiety (p. 765, 834).
Adaptation/Resistance: Resistance to use acts as a significant inhibitor of employees' behavioral intentions (p. 766, 834).
Routinisation: AI adoption is a cognitive and socio-technical process embedded in everyday work (p. 768).
Responsible AI Governance: Redesigning workflows to maintain human agency and decision-making authority alongside AI is necessary (p. 838).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Intention is indirectly influenced by job-replacement anxiety, which heightens resistance (p. 834).

Paper Title: Enhancing Competitiveness in Pakistan: The Role of Green Product Innovation Performance, Artificial Intelligence Adoption, and Government Involvement in Business Strategies
AI Characteristics: AI analyzes extensive datasets and provides actionable insights via predictive analytics (p. 887).
AI Adoption Decision: Found a positive relationship between green innovation performance and the adoption of AI (p. 879, 910).
AI Strategy: Strategic direction enables leaders to prioritize investments that are both financially and ecologically sustainable (p. 916).
AI Use Case Identification: AI is used to provide tailored consumer experiences (p. 887).
Organisational Readiness: Measured via financial resources, quantity of R&D projects, and percentage of R&D personnel (p. 899, 902).
AI Literacy: High academic qualifications (educated mid-career professionals) are essential in theChanging environment (p. 883).
Implementation Coordination: Emphasizes public-private interactions and collaborations in promoting innovation (p. 917).
Capability Development: AIA facilitates the creation of flexible and adaptable organizational capabilities (p. 892).
Responsible AI Governance: Government engagement (assistance, regulatory incentives) significantly moderates the relationship between AIA and competitiveness (p. 879, 908).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AIA significantly contributes to enhancing firm competitiveness and profitability (p. 905).

Paper Title: Ethical frameworks and predictors of ethical artificial intelligence adoption in Kenya’s health sector
AI Adoption Decision: Kenyan health sector AI adoption is still developing, fragmented, and reliant on outside tech (p. 943).
AI Strategy: Proposes Afrocentric ethical policy frameworks inspired by African philosophies like Ubuntu (p. 940, 985).
AI Use Case Identification: Used for predictive diagnosis, predicting epidemics, and managing digital health data (p. 941, 954).
Data Readiness: Data governance (quality, integrity, security) is the strongest predictor of ethical AI adoption (p. 940, 976).
Organisational Readiness: Private hospitals and startups show more structured data procedures than public sector facilities (p. 976, 980).
AI Literacy: Low awareness and ad hoc training on ethical responsibility are major readiness gaps (p. 969, 979, 983).
Implementation Coordination: multi-stakeholder approach involving policymakers, ICT officers, and clinical end-users is required (p. 959).
Capability Development: Strengthening human ethical capacity through interdisciplinary curricula is a foundational pillar (p. 984, 985).
Sensemaking: Ethical culture and guidance from leaders are key to staff viewing ethics as part of their job (p. 978, 980).
Adaptation/Resistance: Staff struggle to critically evaluate tools or identify ethical red flags due to low awareness (p. 969).
Routinisation: Accountability structures (ethics committees) are present but remain unevenly implemented (p. 970, 984).
Responsible AI Governance: Organizational accountability (reporting structures, audits) is a significant predictor of ethical adoption (p. 940, 984).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Ethical AI adoption aims to improve care accuracy without compromising patient rights (p. 971, 985).

Paper Title: Ethical implications of artificial intelligence in accounting: A framework for responsible ai adoption in multinational corporations in Jordan
AI Characteristics: Features include automated data entry, optical character recognition (OCR), and anomaly detection (p. 1006).
Task Fit: AI automates transaction validation, risk analysis, and detail testing in accounting systems (p. 1006).
AI Adoption Decision: Adoption is influenced by Performance/Effort Expectancy, Social Influence, and Facilitating Conditions (p. 1025-1029).
AI Strategy: Framework recommends formulating a long-term ethical strategy to guide responsible integration (p. 1041).
AI Use Case Identification: Applications include fraud detection, tax optimization, and management control systems (p. 1006, 998).
Data Readiness: Management of highly confidential financial information necessitates rigorous data security protocols (p. 1009, 1043).
Organisational Readiness: Older systems may lack architectural framework for AI, requiring significant integration effort (p. 1010).
AI Literacy: Training should prioritize responsible utilization, ethical decision-making, and understanding bias (p. 1043).
Implementation Coordination: Recommends establishing ethical review boards with experts from various disciplines (p. 1043).
Capability Development: Recurring need to develop experts with dual expertise in both accounting and AI (p. 1009).
Sensemaking: Transparency regarding AI's function in decision-making is essential for building user trust (p. 1014, 1015).
Adaptation/Resistance: Resistance arises from fears of human displacement and skepticism regarding computer conclusions (p. 1011).
Routinisation: AI shifts focus from mundane tasks to data-driven analysis and strategic decision-making (p. 1007).
Responsible AI Governance: Transparency and data privacy are the most significant positive influences on AI use (p. 1040).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI improves operational efficiency, reduced time/effort waste, and consistency in auditing (p. 1007).

Paper Title: Evaluation and adoption of artificial intelligence in the retail industry
AI Characteristics: coversinterlinked technologies: data mining, ML, speech/image recognition, and sentiment analysis (p. 1069).
Task Fit: AI is particularly beneficial for product pricing, promotion, and marketing budget allocation (p. 1066).
AI Adoption Decision: Retailers prioritize technology and organization context (controllable) over external environment (uncontrollable) (p. 1063, 1094).
AI Strategy: Recommends adopting strategies for data management to obtain solutions for value creation (p. 1066).
AI Use Case Identification: Used for chatbots and personalized consumer journey maps based on physical location (p. 1066, 1075).
Data Readiness: Data usefulness and the difficulty of data acquisition are the top two critical factors (p. 1083, 1092).
Organisational Readiness: Organizational change capability is a critical factor for applying AI effectively (p. 1083, 1093, 1096).
AI Literacy: Ongoing communication, education, and training are prioritized to reduce adoption failure risk (p. 1100).
Implementation Coordination: Cross-departmental collaboration is necessary to propose innovative business models (p. 1102).
Sensemaking: Top management prioritizes business performance (customer value) over system functional efficiency (p. 1063, 1095, 1104).
Routinisation: AI adoption in Taiwan’s retail industry is noted as being in its infancy (p. 1067).
Responsible AI Governance: Laws and regulations influence adoption, though internal controllable factors are deemed more important (p. 1077, 1094).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI application yields substantial benefits and maintains sustainable competitive advantage (p. 1064, 1066).

Paper Title: Exploring success factors that impact artificial intelligence adoption on technological drivers and managerial capabilities
AI Adoption Decision: Government involvement emerged as a critical external facilitator that significantly enhances AI adoption outcomes in Higher Education Institutions (p. 2).
AI Strategy: Aligns with Vision 2030 digital transformation goals to strengthen institutional performance and higher education outcomes (p. 3).
Data Readiness: Big data utilization (β=0.09) and trust/security mechanisms (β=0.36) significantly enable the technological infrastructure required for adoption (p. 15).
Organisational Readiness: Managerial capability exerts a strong positive influence on AI adoption (β=0.29); traditional factors like support alone were insufficient without technological integration (p. 15, 16).
Capability Development: Integrated digital platforms and big data enhance managers' ability to coordinate, plan, and execute strategic decisions (p. 15).
Routinisation: Identifies an implementation gap where managers struggle to translate formal readiness structures into tangible capabilities (p. 14).
Responsible AI Governance: Finds that organizations rely on regulatory clarity and institutional support before fully leveraging AI technologies (p. 16).

Paper Title: Exploring the Readiness of Organisations to Adopt Artificial Intelligence
Task Fit: Fits the front-end planning phase by enabling data-driven analyses, predictive insights, and improved decision-making to reduce project failure (p. 5).
AI Adoption Decision: Government support, senior management support, and employee attitudes are the top three factors facilitating organisational readiness (p. 2).
AI Strategy: Requires public organisations to map their strategies with Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 long-term plans (p. 3).
Organisational Readiness: Readiness is defined via maturity (culture, resources, processes) and absorptive capacity; maturity directly increases the ability to assimilate AI (p. 10, 15).
Capability Development: Absorptive capacity measures the organization's learning and innovation capacity, allowing it to apply external AI knowledge to performance (p. 12, 14).
Adaptation/Resistance: Employees often misunderstand AI advantages, fearing job replacement, which constitutes the most significant challenge to readiness (p. 15, 16).
Responsible AI Governance: Government support includes establishing the rules, regulations, policies, and legal frameworks necessary to develop innovation (p. 14).

Paper Title: Generative AI Adoption in B2B Firms: Ethical Governance, Innovation Capabilities, and Long-Term Competitive Performance
AI Characteristics: Machine learning models capable of producing new, context-specific content rather than merely classifying data (p. 2).
Task Fit: Augments human sellers by generating tailored proposals, email drafts, and product descriptions in daily sales workflows (p. 2, 28).
AI Adoption Decision: GenAI adoption is positively associated with performance but plays a complementary rather than dominant role in the system (p. 2).
Organisational Readiness: Exploitative innovation is directly associated with performance, while exploratory innovation's effect operates indirectly through GenAI adoption (p. 2).
Routinisation: Experimentation becomes more performance-relevant when translated into digitally enabled routines (p. 2).
Responsible AI Governance: Ethical governance is the strongest correlate of long-term performance, positioning responsible conduct as a core organisational capability (p. 2, 22).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: GenAI adoption accounts for substantial variance in sustainable performance (R2=0.823) when aligned with governance and innovation (p. 17, 21).

Paper Title: Generative AI for Sustainable Development in the Construction Industry Exploring barriers and strategies
AI Characteristics: Enabled by neural network architectures like GANs and transformer models to create novel text, image, and code content (p. 303).
AI Adoption Decision: Identifies "Unclear Legal Liability," "Lack of Explainability," and "Lack of Accuracy" as the most significant industry adoption barriers (p. 302).
Data Readiness: Firms often lack the infrastructure to generate, clean, and organize the high-quality training data required for GenAI (p. 305).
Organisational Readiness: Identifies a passive industry "wait-and-see" stance, prioritizing external government-led initiatives over internal change for adoption (p. 302).
Adaptation/Resistance: Psychological barriers include fear of displacement due to automation (mean=3.595) and resistance to change (mean=3.405) (p. 317, 321).
Responsible AI Governance: High significance is placed on developing output validation mechanisms and clear legal frameworks to handle AI-related disputes (p. 324, 325).

Paper Title: Generative AI in Developing Countries: Adoption Factors in the Vietnamese Public Sector
AI Characteristics: Probabilistic models generating unique responses that blur authorship and complicate responsibility attribution (p. 357).
AI Adoption Decision: Identifies an "AI accountability vacuum"—regulatory ambiguity and unclear responsibility—as a specific environmental constraint (p. 355).
Organisational Readiness: Highlights significant capacity constraints, including absent strategies, limited budgets, weak workflow integration, and inadequate training (p. 355).
AI Literacy: Users interact easily but lack prompt engineering and judgment skills to detect hallucinations or data leakage (p. 372).
Adaptation/Resistance: Reframes resistance not as technophobia but as a rational response to structural voids and capacity gaps (p. 355, 373).
Routinisation: Bottom-up experimentation (shadow adoption) occurs because GenAI is not yet embedded in formal organizational routines (p. 355, 372).

Paper Title: Generative artificial intelligence adoption for achieving supply chain efficiency, circularity and sustainability: An empirical study
AI Adoption Decision: Technology readiness (TR) has a significant positive impact on GenAI adoption (β = 0.224) (p. 438, 446).
Organisational Readiness: Treats technology readiness (optimism, discomfort, innovativeness, insecurity) as an internal organisational stimulus driving adoption (p. 438, 443).
Routinisation: Early stage results show mismatches between GenAI capabilities and existing supply chain processes (p. 447).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: GenAI significantly mediates circular and sustainable supply chain performance, but its impact on efficiency was insignificant (p. 446, 447).

Paper Title: Government adoption of generative artificial intelligence and ambidextrous innovation
AI Adoption Decision: Adoption is positively influenced by relative advantage, compatibility, department leader support, and organisational readiness (p. 498).
Organisational Readiness: Organisational readiness (financial resources, experts, culture) is positively correlated with adoption; leader support is critical for prioritizing funds (p. 469, 475).
Capability Development: Adoption significantly influences both exploratory and exploitative innovation behaviors within government departments (p. 490).
Adaptation/Resistance: "Perceived Threat"—the belief that jobs can be replaced—acts as a factor negatively moderating innovation outcomes (p. 479, 488).

Paper Title: Healthcare Providers’ Perspectives on Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) Adoption, Adaptation, Assimilation, and Use in the United States
AI Adoption Decision: Organizations of participants with doctorate degrees were statistically more likely to have officially adopted AI (p. 532).
AI Use Case Identification: Most common uses are report writing (43.1%), research (27.7%), and patient care (26.2%) (p. 534).
Organisational Readiness: Adoption is primarily led by top-level executive leadership, though 23.2% of respondents were unaware of the leader (p. 532).
AI Literacy: Formal training is low (42.4%), mostly focusing on basic orientation rather than clinical or technical use (p. 532, 533).
Adaptation/Resistance: Key barriers include lack of knowledge (24.7%), fear of job loss (16.9%), and staff resistance to change (6.5%) (p. 535).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI is perceived as most useful for patient care and management by 86.9% of providers (p. 532).

Paper Title: Exploring the Determinants of Artificial Intelligence Adoption Intention in the SMEs of United Arab Emirates
AI Adoption Decision: Top management support (β=0.48) and competitive pressure (β=0.47) are the strongest drivers, exceeding technological perceptions (p. 570, 584).
Organisational Readiness: Readiness is leadership-centric; employee capability enhances intention but is secondary to management support and resource allocation (p. 587).
Adaptation/Resistance: Leadership endorsement fosters alignment across multicultural workforces, thereby reducing resistance to AI initiatives (p. 587).
Responsible AI Governance: Government regulations are significantly and positively associated with AI adoption intention (β=0.43, p=0.000) (p. 584, 587).

Paper Title: IDENTIFICATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ADOPTION DETERMINANTS AFFECTING HUMAN RESOURCE MANAGEMENT EFFECTIVENESS IN THE INDIAN INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY SECTOR
AI Characteristics: Incorporates automated predefined tasks and predictive analytics for workforce management (p. 31).
Task Fit: Streamlines HR functions including recruitment, selection, and performance monitoring (p. 31, 37).
AI Adoption Decision: Significantly influenced by technological readiness, competitive pressure, and security/privacy concerns, rather than formal organizational preparedness (p. 34, 35, 38).
AI Strategy: AI adoption acts as a mediating mechanism connecting contextual enablers to HRM outcomes (p. 30, 36).
AI Use Case Identification: Identifies applications in talent acquisition and workforce planning (p. 31).
Data Readiness: Finds that data availability and infrastructure are critical for supporting implementation (p. 34).
Organisational Readiness: Observes that general perceptions of preparedness are insufficient without technological enablers and infrastructure (p. 34, 38).
AI Literacy: Identifies technical skill as a necessary technological readiness component (p. 32).
Implementation Coordination: Coalesces competitive dynamics, technological capability, and governance mechanisms to produce outcomes (p. 36, 37).
Responsible AI Governance: Security and privacy concerns regarding data protection and ethical use significantly impact adoption (p. 32, 38).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Significantly improves HRM effectiveness in terms of decision quality, operational efficiency, and strategic outcomes (p. 31, 38).

Paper Title: Information-analytical system for evaluating artificial intelligence readiness and adoption in enterprises
Task Fit: Applied across production, development, logistics, decision-making, and service functions (p. 4).
AI Adoption Decision: Stages include assessing implementation possibility and managerial understanding of that potential (p. 7, 21).
AI Strategy: Strategy model aligns AIA feasibility with achieving sustainable business results (p. 1, 14).
AI Use Case Identification: Framework includes criteria for exploring potential organizational benefits and use case possibilities (p. 9, 21).
Data Readiness: Critically evaluates data quality, availability, and management throughout the AI lifecycle (p. 10, 21).
Organisational Readiness: Readiness is context-sensitive, influenced by financial stability, innovation capacity, and top management support (p. 2, 9).
AI Literacy: Emphasizes increasing digital literacy and employee analytical skills via human resource management (p. 10).
Implementation Coordination: Requires cross-departmental coordination to define, document, and monitor work toward AI goals (p. 10).
Responsible AI Governance: Incorporates ethical principles and regulatory compliance into the evaluation framework for responsible adoption (p. 10, 21).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: High adoption potential coupled with managerial understanding fosters higher productivity, efficiency, and competitiveness (p. 1, 14, 21).

Paper Title: Integrating SAP-LAP with a Bayesian Best–Worst Method to Assess Generative AI Adoption
AI Characteristics: Classifies tools including LLMs, generative design platforms, and forecasting/simulation models (p. 243).
AI Adoption Decision: Prioritizes barriers across technological, organizational, and environmental contexts using Bayesian BWM (p. 245, 255).
AI Strategy: Aligns GenAI initiatives with global sustainability mandates and UN SDGs (p. 241, 243).
AI Use Case Identification: Identifies use cases in emissions forecasting, logistics route management, and materials consumption reduction (p. 243, 254).
Data Readiness: Identifies data quality and availability as the most significant technological barriers to effective modeling (p. 247, 257).
Organisational Readiness: Identifies limited financial resources and human capital as major organizational barriers, especially for SMEs (p. 247, 255).
AI Literacy: Shortage of skilled professionals and AI-literate talent is a common barrier (p. 247, 254).
Implementation Coordination: Outcomes are contingent upon coordinating technological readiness, regulatory support, and supply chain collaboration (p. 254).
