Adaptation/Resistance: Identifies employee resistance to change as a significant organizational barrier (p. 247, 257).
Responsible AI Governance: Emphasizes managing regulatory hurdles and data governance frameworks to manage privacy and legal risks (p. 251, 260).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Optimizes resource utilization, reduces waste, and improves environmental performance across the triple bottom line (p. 243, 254).

Paper Title: Investigating GenAI Adoption Readiness of Healthcare SMEs in Philippines
Task Fit: Potential to support documentation, summarization, and administrative tasks (p. 2).
AI Adoption Decision: Shaped by the interaction of structural barriers and supportive enablers across four dimensions (p. 3, 10).
AI Strategy: Strategy requires alignment with national digital health initiatives and standards (p. 3, 10).
Data Readiness: Linked to weak infrastructure, paper-based workflows, and fragmented records (p. 10, 11).
Organisational Readiness: Major barriers include constrained budgets, underdeveloped governance, and low confidence in technology (p. 2, 11).
AI Literacy: Identifies limited digital literacy as a primary workforce readiness barrier (p. 2, 10).
Implementation Coordination: Institutional partnerships with universities and government help fill internal capability gaps (p. 3, 10).
Capability Development: Workforce training and mentoring are key enablers for effective tool use (p. 10, 11).
Adaptation/Resistance: Staff overload and low confidence can increase resistance when systems are perceived as disruptive (p. 3, 11).
Responsible AI Governance: Identifies underdeveloped governance, weak privacy practices, and unclear accountability as major implementation risks (p. 2, 11).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Aims for safe, locally appropriate, and sustainable service delivery in low-resource healthcare settings (p. 2, 12).

Paper Title: Knowledge Management-Based Artificial Intelligence (AI) Adoption in Construction SMEs
AI Adoption Decision: Driven by performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and behavioral intentions (p. 2, 5, 6).
Organisational Readiness: Perceived organizational knowledge and openness to innovation positively impact intentions (p. 1, 5).
AI Literacy: Organizational knowledge and employees' capacity to learn operations influence effort expectations (p. 2).
Capability Development: Strengthening knowledge integration capability helps store, extend, and apply knowledge for sustained use (p. 3, 6).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Behavioral intentions and knowledge integration capability significantly predict actual AI use (p. 5, 6).

Paper Title: Navigating complexity A relational perspective on generative AI adoption in government
AI Use Case Identification: Identifies experiments in content generation, quality review, and using operational material for queries (p. 6).
Sensemaking: Adoption involves relational processes where users make sense of technology within their specific context (p. 3, 5).

Paper Title: Navigating institutional and capability barriers in agentic artificial intelligence adoption
AI Characteristics: Advanced systems using specialized AI agents and shared memory to pursue multi-step goals autonomously (p. 5).
AI Adoption Decision: Adoption is shaped by ecosystem maturity and institutional conditions alongside firm readiness (p. 21, 23).
Data Readiness: Fragmented data architectures and inconsistent stewardship in SMEs act as structural barriers (p. 8).
Organisational Readiness: Barriers include political instability, regulatory uncertainty, and high costs of adoption (p. 21).
AI Literacy: Shortage of skilled employees and lack of knowledge about agentic AI are critical internal barriers (p. 7, 21).
Implementation Coordination: Fostering public-private partnerships is recommended to overcome institutional maturity gaps (p. 2, 20).
Capability Development: Requires developing dynamic capabilities (sensing, seizing, reconfiguring) to achieve strategic agility (p. 21).
Responsible AI Governance: Accountability and liability are fundamentally unclear for agentic decisions, increasing legal risks (p. 7, 10).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Aims to provide continuous optimization and adaptive problem-solving across processes (p. 5, 20).

Paper Title: Recommendations for efficient and responsible LLM adoption within industrial software development
Task Fit: Scoping applicability within software engineering tasks is a key best practice for adoption (p. 2, 25).
AI Adoption Decision: High level of practitioner agreement found for developed adoption recommendations (p. 2, 33).
AI Strategy: Strategy emphasizes scoping applicability to define the boundary of LLM use cases (p. 18, 26).
AI Use Case Identification: Developed RAG POC tool specifically for generating stakeholder analysis artifacts (p. 12).
Organisational Readiness: Stakeholder satisfaction with generated outputs should be part of the evaluation criteria (p. 2, 25).
AI Literacy: Practitioners need skills in prompt engineering and understanding how models work (p. 20, 23).
Implementation Coordination: Knowledge-sharing activities like seminars and specialized training are crucial for users (p. 25).
Routinisation: Integrates LLMs by restructuring business processes to create room for the tools (p. 25, 26).
Responsible AI Governance: Recommends developing human oversight and validation mechanisms to enhance regulatory compliance (p. 2, 25, 28).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Practitioners prioritize output usefulness over strict accuracy to support overall workflows (p. 24, 26).

Paper Title: Responsible Flexibility in the Generative Artificial Intelligence Adoption
AI Adoption Decision: Organizations position themselves along a responsibility–agility continuum (p. 489, 510).
AI Strategy: Strategic flexibility translates responsible innovation principles into actionable routines (p. 493, 502).
AI Use Case Identification: Sensing phase includes scans of qualified strategic opportunities and red-flag risks (p. 501, 515).
Organisational Readiness: Responsibility Index measures formal governance infrastructure and stakeholder interface transparency (p. 510, 519).
Implementation Coordination: Seizing phase requires transparently disclosing trade-offs and mitigation plans to stakeholders (p. 501, 516).
Capability Development: Integrates dynamic capabilities to reconfigure resources ethically for long-term advantage (p. 492, 493).
Sensemaking: Structures risk-opportunity mapping to avoid learning myopia and maintain balance (p. 512, 515).
Adaptation/Resistance: Institutional resistance and cultural stickiness are identified as barriers progress (p. 504, 516).
Routinisation: Transforming phase reconfigures routines based on pilot results to institutionalize practices (p. 503, 516).
Responsible AI Governance: Formal ethics oversight and regulatory compliance (e.g., EU AI Act) are integrated into workflows (p. 498, 499).
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Responsible flexibility acts as a core competence and source of resilience and trust (p. 489, 511).

Paper Title: Speaking About Artificial Intelligence for Sustainability—How Employees’ Perception of Credibility Shapes Their Initial Attitudes Toward AI Adoption
AI Characteristics: Defined as computer systems performing tasks typically requiring human intelligence, often utilizing deep learning and large datasets.
Task Fit: Primarily evaluated for knowledge management tasks within a data-driven organizational context.
AI Adoption Decision: Finds intention is influenced by the communicated rationale (ecological, social, or economic) and individuals' pre-existing sustainability attitudes.
AI Strategy: Suggests transparently communicating economic benefits alongside ecological and social advantages to maintain positive initial employee attitudes.
Organisational Readiness: Company trustworthiness (high vs. low) did not significantly affect message credibility or initial attitudes toward the technology.
AI Literacy: Self-reports indicated that most participants already had a relatively good understanding of what "AI" means.
Sensemaking: Ecological and social rationales were perceived as less credible than economic ones, as they conflict with general expectations of corporate profit-seeking.
Adaptation/Resistance: Insufficient initial acceptance may give rise to resistance, limiting potential organizational sustainability contributions.
Responsible AI Governance: Recommends value-sensitive design and participatory methods to incorporate user needs and ensure the AI system is designed trustworthily.
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: High attitudinal acceptance can foster usage and internalization, potentially leading to positive performance outcomes for the organization.

Paper Title: The Jevons Paradox in the AI era: Artificial intelligence adoption for enhancing environmental sustainability at the firm level
AI Characteristics: Refers to intelligent systems involving core technologies such as machine learning, neural networks, computer vision, and natural language processing.
Task Fit: AI optimizes operational productivity by streamlining production processes through predictive maintenance and intelligent automation.
AI Adoption Decision: Influenced by firm-specific characteristics like age, size, and capital intensity, as well as provincial environmental regulations.
AI Strategy: Proposes that targeted policies should leverage AI for decarbonization while actively managing scale-driven rebound effects.
AI Use Case Identification: Identifies applications across smart education, government, finance, retail, healthcare, transportation, and environmental protection.
Data Readiness: Recognizes that firms often lack the necessary infrastructure to generate and organize high-quality training data for modeling.
Organisational Readiness: State-owned enterprises and capital-intensive firms demonstrate a stronger ability to translate AI adoption into emission intensity reductions.
Capability Development: AI adoption significantly enhances total factor productivity and serves as a powerful catalyst for firm-level green innovation.
Routinisation: AI adoption expands the overall production scale and increases total resource consumption, resulting in a net increase in absolute emissions.
Responsible AI Governance: Stricter provincial environmental regulations effectively attenuate the emissions-increasing effect driven by AI-enabled production growth.
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Reveals an "AI Jevons Paradox": AI adoption significantly reduces carbon emission intensity but leads to an absolute increase in total carbon emissions.

Paper Title: The effect of supply chain learning in mitigating the challenges to adopting artificial intelligence for supply chain sustainability
AI Characteristics: Characterized as intelligent machines performing cognitive functions like learning and problem-solving to sense and respond autonomously.
Task Fit: AI facilitates sustainability by enabling operational optimization, carbon footprint minimization, and demand prediction.
AI Adoption Decision: Adoption is restricted by various technological, organizational, human, and institutional challenges.
AI Strategy: Recommends that firms integrate supply chain learning strategies to accomplish new strategic operations like AI-enabled digitalization.
AI Use Case Identification: Utilized for inventory management, pollution control alerts, and reducing product shortages.
Data Readiness: Poor data quality and lack of data management resources rank as the second most significant technological challenge.
Organisational Readiness: Lack of leadership support and high costs are identified as critical organizational bottlenecks to readiness.
AI Literacy: Shortage of AI talent and lack of machine learning knowledge are the highest-ranked human challenges.
Implementation Coordination: Requires building strong interconnectedness and synchronization of manufacturing processes with third-party collaborators and supply chain partners.
Capability Development: Supply chain learning (e.g., transformational leadership, governance) develops collective knowledge and competencies for successful implementation.
Sensemaking: Lack of awareness regarding performance benefits is a human barrier that can hinder adoption decisions.
Adaptation/Resistance: Workers may resist AI due to uncertainty about status-quo shifts and fear of replacement.
Routinisation: Employs machine-learning algorithms for automatic processing in inventory management and supply chain advisory systems.
Responsible AI Governance: Requires independent institutions to monitor ethical aspects and governance frameworks to assess societal impact.
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI adoption improves operational efficiency, transaction transparency, and facilitates long-term supply chain sustainability.

Paper Title: The risk-mitigation effects of artificial intelligence adoption: Evidence from executive misconduct
AI Characteristics: Characterized by high computational power, big data analytics, and real-time monitoring capabilities.
Task Fit: AI automates information processing and standardizes decision workflows to improve governance quality.
AI Adoption Decision: Influenced by firm characteristics including size, leverage, profitability, and institutional ownership.
AI Strategy: Embedding AI into day-to-day processes supports the normalization and formalization of corporate governance.
AI Use Case Identification: Identified use cases include financial reporting review, internal audit sampling, and procurement monitoring.
Organisational Readiness: Larger and older firms exhibit distinct structural challenges in compliance compared to smaller entities.
Capability Development: Adoption lowers agency costs and significantly enhances internal control capacity over executive behavior.
Routinisation: Strategic AI investment institutionalizes digital governance and makes firm cost structures more rigid.
Responsible AI Governance: AI application significantly reduces executive misconduct across incidence, frequency, and monetary penalty amounts.
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI adoption reduces firms' cost of debt financing and significantly enhances total factor productivity.

Paper Title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence Adoption on Knowledge Creation Processes in Ecosystem-Based Business Models
AI Characteristics: Uses deep learning algorithms capable of performing cognitive functions traditionally associated with human intelligence.
Task Fit: Complements human cognitive limitations in managing complex, multiobjective decisions and handling explicit knowledge.
AI Adoption Decision: Adoption intensity follows an inverted U-shaped relationship with ecosystem sustainability.
AI Strategy: Managers should implement phased AI rollouts with continuous monitoring of knowledge creation metrics.
AI Use Case Identification: Used to identify external resources and optimize routine operational processes within the ecosystem.
Data Readiness: Excessive use of AI increases potential risks regarding data privacy and security.
Organisational Readiness: Well-established firms where management holds significant shares are better positioned to effectively utilize AI.
AI Literacy: Investment in training is needed to facilitate effective collaboration between employees and AI agents.
Implementation Coordination: Requires established cross-functional AI governance teams and collaboration with external partners like suppliers or customers.
Capability Development: Moderate adoption acts as a catalyst for knowledge creation and dynamic capability enhancement.
Sensemaking: Data processing opacity can lead to human suspicion and distrust, known as algorithm aversion.
Adaptation/Resistance: Excessive reliance suppresses human creativity and can result in organizational inertia.
Routinisation: Progress in data processing and pattern recognition enables rapid rapid knowledge dissemination and application.
Responsible AI Governance: Proposes industry-specific ethics frameworks and tiered guidelines to preserve knowledge ecosystems.
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Moderate AI adoption enhances knowledge flows and sustainability performance, but over-reliance triggers a decline.

Paper Title: Towards Human-AI Symbiosis: Designing an Artificial Intelligence Adoption Framework
AI Characteristics: Capabilities include learning from data and performing tasks autonomously through machine learning and natural language processing.
Task Fit: AI enables cognitive automation and augments human analytics within a symbiosis partnership.
AI Adoption Decision: Follows five decision stages (knowledge to confirmation) influenced by technological, organizational, and environmental factors.
AI Strategy: Requires a defined architecture strategy and alignment with organizational digital transformation and sustainability goals.
AI Use Case Identification: Identified applications include data curation, process automation, and event management (AIOps).
Data Readiness: Relies on high quality/amount of data, scalable infrastructure, and organizational-wide data assets.
Organisational Readiness: Readiness is driven by top management support, innovative culture, and access to competencies.
AI Literacy: Skill shortages are addressed through training on AI tools, platforms, and principles knowledge.
Implementation Coordination: Supported by communities of practice and external providers when specific AI knowledge is not internal.
Capability Development: Organizations must build development, platform, and operational expertise for successful implementation.
Sensemaking: Champions and real-world examples help members grasp the importance and benefits of AI adoption.
Adaptation/Resistance: Barriers include user resistance, the knowledge-attitude-practice gap, and talent issues.
Routinisation: MLOps and CI/CD concepts embed AI solutions into routine production environments.
Responsible AI Governance: Integrates fairness, accountability, transparency, and explainability into teams' daily work and governance bodies.
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Adoption aims to achieve financial benefits, competitive advantage, and faster evidence-based decision-making.

Paper Title: Towards a Socio-specific Artificial Intelligence Adoption Framework
AI Characteristics: Features include computer-based systems capable of learning, reasoning, and autonomous action.
Task Fit: Supports data-driven entities through forward-looking analysis and automated decision-making.
AI Adoption Decision: Moves through five stages—knowledge, persuasion, decision, implementation, confirmation—involving weighing advantages and disadvantages.
AI Strategy: Adoption is a continuum requiring an innovative culture and the constant removal of barriers.
Data Readiness: Relies on data quality and sufficient data structures to train proper models.
Organisational Readiness: Readiness is influenced by resources, competencies, culture, and active top management support.
AI Literacy: Training on tools, platforms, and concepts for both employees and management is a key enabler.
Implementation Coordination: Implementation involves business units and potentially utilizing support from external providers.
Capability Development: Building capabilities is achieved through training and leverages analytics competence centers.
Sensemaking: Real-life examples from demos and pilots help boost confidence in AI benefits.
Adaptation/Resistance: Implementation challenges include user resistance and talent issues.
Routinisation: Embedded through CI/CD concepts and machine learning operations to ensure smooth flows.
Responsible AI Governance: Incorporates fairness, accountability, transparency, and explainability (FAT) into daily team work and governance processes.
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: AI adoption delivers strategic organizational value and improved decision-making quality.

Paper Title: Trust Dynamics and Economic Implications of Generative AI Adoption in Digital Journalism
AI Characteristics: Generative AI involves automated content production that affects established concepts of authorship and accountability.
Task Fit: Automating routine tasks like transcription and summarization assists human editorial judgment.
AI Adoption Decision: Organizations choose between covert use, transparent rollout, or proactive ethical positioning under economic strain.
AI Strategy: AI integration functions as a governance-mediated signal interpreted by audiences in economic terms.
AI Use Case Identification: Deployed for production efficiency, production cycles, and automated content drafting.
Organisational Readiness: Success depends on institutional managerial and communicational capacity regarding technological decisions.
AI Literacy: Professionals show conditional acceptance when AI implementation is transparent and maintains professionalism.
Sensemaking: Audiences interpret organizational changes and AI use as indicators of institutional goals and values.
Adaptation/Resistance: Covert or undisclosed use contributes to narratives of deception and severe erosion of audience trust.
Responsible AI Governance: High transparency and ethical framing (defending integrity) are primary drivers of audience loyalty.
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Weak governance corresponds with increased engagement instability (ERI) and severe revenue contraction.

Paper Title: The Adoption and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence Chatbots in Public Organizations: Evidence from U.S. State Governments
AI Characteristics: Chatbots use natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval with text-based or voice-driven interfaces.
Task Fit: Chatbots provide 24/7 informational assistance, handle FAQs, and perform transactional public services.
AI Adoption Decision: Driven by ease of use, relative advantage, external COVID-19 shock, and individual past experiences.
AI Strategy: Agencies MODERNIZED customer service through automation and self-service goals.
AI Use Case Identification: Applied in unemployment insurance, taxes, social welfare, education, and public health.
Data Readiness: Requires knowledge-base creation using website analytics, back-end data, and FAQ content.
Organisational Readiness: Readiness is facilitated by leadership's willingness to try new things and an innovative culture.
AI Literacy: Agencies often lack the technology skills to build and manage chatbots independently.
Implementation Coordination: Involves cross-agency interaction, collaboration with IT vendors, and aligning stakeholder expectations.
Capability Development: Staff members learn to monitor and adjust chatbots through training provided by IT partners.
Sensemaking: Analytics metadata enable agencies to tailor responses to users' shifting information needs.
Adaptation/Resistance: Challenges are managed via soft launches and handling questions that chatbots could not initially answer.
Routinisation: Reallocating existing staff ensures long-term chatbot management and sustainability after pilot periods.
Responsible AI Governance: Adheres to safety regulations by ensuring current usage does not require personally identifiable information.
Stakeholder Value & Organisational Perfo: Reduces administrative burdens, improves citizen interactions, and decreases service delivery costs.
